The founder's numbers are pinned to the launch era (the founder's gap-11 rule): the YC company page as captured on
2025-10-16, the partnership terms page of 2025-10-15 and the Launch YC post of 2025-10-19. Anything later is under

## The founder-emulation items

1. **Who (practitioner `agent`).** YC-C names hotel groups with "call centers and central reservation departments";
   YC-L's video features front-desk staff at a Munich hotel. *My choice:* the reservation agent, central office or
   front desk, who sees the missed-call list. Segment: hotel groups in Germany with a central office or call center.
2. **When (circumstance, occasion, window).** YC-L's "After hours. During peak hours. On holidays." *My choice:* the
   occasion "reservation shift", window the last 7 days (calls come in on every shift; spec 120's "every shift" -> 7
   DAYS), Frequency 5 to 7 days out of 7.
3. **Who pays (decision-maker `director`, Buyer and payer, Purchase friction).** TERMS addresses the hotel group;
   YC-L asks to "book a 10-minute call if you lead a hotel group". *My choice:* the revenue or reservations director
   decides, the hotel's owner has to agree. Purchase friction tests "A data protection review of guest calls" (German
   hotels handle guests' card and personal data on the call); my choice, no source names it.
4. **Mechanism.** YC-C: missed calls forwarded to Codyco, the AI answers, bookings appear in the PMS. Compatibility
   tests call forwarding (the mechanism needs it); Adoption friction tests letting the AI answer in the hotel's voice.
5. **Cost, price, ability.** As in the table. Reading `budget` by the engine (a percent of calls against euros).
6. **Commitment.** TERMS and YC-L: the paid, money-back pilot at one location. The step carries its number ("pay
   €3,000 for a money-back pilot at one hotel"), the gap-8 check.

## The respondents

No first-person account by a German reservation agent or revenue director was found in public (no HN thread; the
site's quotes are curated testimonials). **Every person is the author's invention**, no real person's name is used,
and each is built on the public facts named here.

Reservation agents (Parts 1 and 2):
- Lena Hoffmann: a trade-fair Saturday in a Munich central office; built on YC-L ("During peak hours") and the Munich
  hotel YC-L features.
- Murat Yilmaz: a check-in rush at the desk; YC-L's "peak hours".
- Chiara Russo: a group whose call center already answers after hours (YC-C: "Even with call centers..."); her pain is
  group emails, so Importance and Current solution go against the founder.
- Jonas Weber: alone on a Sunday desk; YC-L's "On holidays" / after hours.
- Aylin Demir: an old phone system that cannot forward (Compatibility only_with_help); the author's.
- Tobias Brandl: the sceptic who will not hand guests to an AI (Relative advantage negative, Adoption no); the author's.
- Elif Kaya: weekend abandoned calls seen on Monday; YC-L's "After hours".
- Daniel Okonkwo: rates pushed wrong to agencies matter more (Importance against); the author's.
- Mehmet Arslan: a vague story, GUESSED. Katarina Novak: a story chip, GUESSED.
- Florian Gruber, Nadia Haddad: gate No (no unanswered booking call in the 7 days).

Revenue directors (COMMERCIAL_B2B link, Part 3): Stefanie Wagner (6%), Andreas Keller (4%, below the founder's 5%),
Roberto Bianchi (8%), Ingrid Lindholm (2%, a call center covers after hours), Karim Benali (does not know his rate;
YC-L's "Free AI Strategy Workshop" and SITE's free test number as his ask), Petra Vogel (5%), Hannes Moser (nothing,
would not pay), Joanna Wiśniewska (10% at resort hotels in high season). The value boxes are percents of the calls, in
the founder's unit and period; the price picks are two codes, the pilot's rung and the licence's rung, each placed
against the founder's €3,000 and €1,000.

## Status today

Same idea (SITE, 2026-10-22): "Turn missed hotel calls into paid bookings.", widened to payments, invoices and
handovers; "Running at 15+ hotel groups" (the launch said 7); "€10k+ bookings written directly into the PMS". **No
public price today** (SITE and /faq show none); the €3,000 pilot terms remain the only priced source.

## Open (what could not be sourced, and the workarounds)

- **The licence amount** was never public. €1,000 to €1,500 per hotel a month is the operator's reading of the pilot's
  monthly rate (above). Treat the plan step's reading as a reading of that derivation.
- **Dollars or euros.** YC-L says "$5,000", YC-C "€5,000" for the same hotel; the pilot fee is in euros and the company
  is in Munich, so the entry is in euros. The market is DE, and the golden corpus's rule U (US only) is a note.
- **The "> 8 hotels" / "10 hotels" roll-out threshold** in TERMS and YC-L disagree; the entry does not use it.
- **Job titles.** Neither the agent nor the director is named in public; both are my choices (items 1 and 3).
- **The 5% is the founders' claim** for "the best" offices; no independent figure was sought.
- **UPFRONT_THEN has no "credited" or "money-back" flag**; the fee is a plain up-front amount (header).

insights.line: What would make it worth more

whys.g1: Ingrid and Andreas both say so few calls are lost that paying is hard to justify, which I would recognise as one reason, the name is plain, and Hannes's refusal over guests and reputation and Karim's not knowing his rate rightly stay outside it.
whys.g2: There is no junk, explicit or off-topic answer on this line, so nothing needed keeping out.

whys.g1: With no groups formed, nothing is misplaced, and leaving these apart is what I would do because the four answers give different reasons: the licence costing more than the missed bookings bring in, not knowing the miss rate, guests refusing a robot, and an owner who would agree after seeing it run.
whys.g2: There is no junk, explicit or off-topic answer on this line, and all four speak to what would slow or settle the purchase, so nothing needed keeping out.

whys.g1: With only two answers saying very different things, one wanting proof on its own numbers because the call center covers after hours and the other naming a managing director who would agree quickly, leaving each on its own is what I would do, and no existing group was missed.
whys.g2: There is no junk answer on this line, and both answers speak to whether the pilot would be agreed and paid for, so nothing had to be kept out.

founder.order_why: The flow runs sensibly from context to problem, idea, buyer and sending, but the agent's problem and idea are written before Keel establishes that a revenue director pays, so I only learn at screen 10 that there are two audiences, and the pilot offer at screen 22 sits apart from the first real step at screens 20-21, where my paid pilot is already the answer.
founder.asked_twice: Screens 3 and 4 share one heading and question; screens 20-21 (first real step, a paid pilot) and 22 (Offer a pilot?) cover the same decision; screens 10-11 (who decides, who answers) and 14-16 (who else must agree, buyer alignment) overlap on who is involved in the purchase.
founder.missing: How the buying unit works: whether a pilot at one hotel is decided per property or by the group, and how many hotels a group would roll out to, since my price is per hotel and the group's size decides the deal. Also the systems it must connect to, the PMS (OPERA Cloud, Sihot, Apaleo) and the phone setup, as a purchase condition.

COMMERCIAL_B2B.order_why: The flow from screener to idea, lost calls, value, budget, sign-off and data protection is logical, but 'What would take the time in buying Codyco?' sits under a separate 'One more thing' heading just before the final 6 of 6 pilot question, interrupting the count and feeling like it belongs after the close.
COMMERCIAL_B2B.missing: How many hotels in the group and how many reservation calls we handle, whether after-hours calls are already covered by a call center, what a lost booking is worth to us, and how Codyco would connect to our PMS or central reservation system.

screens.why2: The belief and options are plain to me, but the screen has no question and in the bar's "they had to agree last time" I have to work out who "they" is and last time of what.
screens.why3: I sell to hotel groups and know from my own sales calls who has to sign off on a €3,000 pilot.
screens.why4: The three options are distinct and in my words, but a group's managing director (Geschäftsführer), often the real second signature at a hotel group, is missing and there is no other or not-sure escape.
screens.why5: The belief still says what I meant: the revenue director decides and the hotel's owner has to agree.
screens.instead: Skip the repeat pick and show only the belief and test: "The hotel group revenue director decides, and the hotel's owner has to agree. Holds if at least 2 in 3 directors say the owner had to agree the last time they bought something like this."

screens.why1: Straight after who has to agree, asking what could slow or stop the purchase is the obvious next step in how a hotel group buys.
screens.why2: Approvals, reviews and procurement are everyday words for anyone selling to hotel groups, and the question reads clearly the first time.
screens.why3: I sell the pilot to hotel groups, so I know from my own sales conversations what holds a deal up, though the data protection point is my own judgement and not a sourced fact.
screens.why4: The free-text box and the escape chip fit, but the hint's 'switching' is odd for us because we catch missed calls rather than replace a system, and it omits the owner's sign-off or budget.
screens.why5: The belief keeps my data protection review in my own words but adds 'slows the purchase most', a ranking I never claimed, and drops the PMS check and the one-hotel trial I also typed.
screens.instead: What could slow down or stop a hotel group buying this? (Approvals, data protection, PMS checks, a trial first.) Up to 25 words.

screens.why1: Right after I named what could slow a purchase, Keel shows the belief it drew from that answer for me to check, so it is obvious why it is here.
screens.why2: Data protection review, PMS and vendor sign-off are everyday words when selling to German hotel groups, and the belief reads at once.
screens.why3: As the founder who sells to these groups, I know from my own sales calls what holds up a pilot, though which blocker is biggest is still my bet.
screens.why4: The three rows are distinct and in my words, and the data protection one is mine, but "our PMS" slips into the buyer's voice on a founder's screen and the owner's agreement I named as a hurdle is not among them.
screens.why5: The belief keeps my purchase friction word for word, and adding "slows the purchase most" is a fair reading of the belief I wanted tested.

screens.why1: Right after I named what could slow a purchase and checked Keel's wording, it is obvious why I am now asked to pick the one belief to test.
screens.why2: Data protection review, PMS and vendor sign-off are everyday words in selling to a German hotel group, and the belief reads clearly on first pass.
screens.why3: I sell to hotel groups and know from my own sales calls what holds a deal up, though the data protection choice is my judgement rather than a measured fact.
screens.why4: The three options are distinct and in my words, but 'our PMS' speaks from the hotel's side while the screen addresses me, and the bar's 'it' (needed last time and took a long time) fits the review and vendor sign-off more naturally than a quick PMS check.
screens.why5: The belief says exactly what I picked, the data protection review of guest calls as the main brake on the purchase.

screens.why1: After who decides, the price and what could stop a purchase, it is obvious to ask what real step I want from the buyer, and my paid pilot is the natural answer here.
screens.why2: "First real step" and the hint about time, data, money or a signature are clear on first reading, and I can answer at once with my pilot terms.
screens.why3: This is my own sales motion: the €3,000 money-back pilot at one location is in my partnership terms and launch post.
screens.why4: The free-text box takes my answer as typed, and "Leave this out of the study" is a fitting escape for a founder who has no such step to test.
screens.why5: My step is kept word for word, but Keel's belief says "most reservation agents would pay" when I said the revenue or reservations director decides and the owner must agree, and no agent can spend €3,000, so the belief is wrong.
screens.instead: Keep the question and box, and write the belief as: "Most revenue or reservations directors at hotel groups would pay €3,000 now for a money-back pilot at one hotel."

screens.why1: Right after I named the paid pilot as the first real step, it makes sense for Keel to show me the belief it will test and the bar it must clear, as the last of the six commercial checks.
screens.why2: The price and pilot are in my own words and 'reservation agents' is plain to me, but 'Holds if no more than 1 in 3 say probably not or no' takes a second read to see which answers count against the belief.
screens.why3: A reservation agent has no budget and never signs a €3,000 pilot, because that is the revenue or reservations director's job, with the owner's agreement, so the belief is about a decision agents never make.
screens.why4: The screen shows a drafted belief and a bar to accept or edit, with no options, rows, chips or value box to judge.
screens.why5: The pilot, price and money-back terms are kept, but the buyer is wrong: I told Keel the hotel group revenue director decides, and this says most reservation agents would pay.
screens.instead: Most hotel group revenue directors would pay €3,000 now for a money-back pilot at one hotel. Holds if no more than 1 in 3 directors say probably not or no.

screens.why1: Right after setting the paid pilot as the first real step and just before the study goes out, it makes sense to ask whether people can raise their hand for a pilot.
screens.why2: The words are plain and I run pilots myself, but 'Offer a pilot?' does not say whether this is my €3,000 paid pilot or a free sign-up, so I read it twice.
screens.why3: Whether to offer a pilot is my own decision, and the Zero Risk Pilot is already how I sell.
screens.why4: The only control is an optional step with Continue, which is fine as an escape, but it gives me no visible yes or no and no way to tie the offer to my pilot terms.
screens.why5: I typed a €3,000 money-back pilot at one hotel as the commitment, and this bare 'pilot' drops the price and terms, drifting a little from what I said.
screens.instead: Let people ask to join your paid pilot once they have answered: €3,000 up front, money-back, one hotel, up to 8 weeks? (Yes, offer it / No, not in this study)

screens.why1: Choosing how the study is delivered belongs just before launch, but the question asks who should do the asking while the hint says the AI interviewer is unavailable on this account, so the choice feels partly settled before I make it.
screens.why2: The question is plain, but 'this account runs on its own AI' and 'Keel's credits' take a second read, and I have to work out that 'its own AI' means no interviewer voice for my respondents.
screens.why3: As the founder I know how my reservation agents and directors can be reached, and I can decide whether they should tap through or be interviewed.
screens.why4: The picked answer 'Lock and record the face Keel preselects' describes a mechanic rather than who asks, and it sits oddly beside a hint saying people will read and tap, so the choice between a face, an AI voice and no interviewer is not distinct.
screens.why5: Nothing here changes what I typed about Codyco, the hotel groups or the pilot, because the screen is only about how the study is delivered.
screens.instead: How should people answer your questions? Options: They read and tap (included on this account) / An AI interviewer talks with them (uses Keel credits).

screens.why1: Choosing how people answer belongs just before sending, but it comes straight after 'Who should ask them your questions?' and overlaps with it, and the kicker says 'SENT' as if the study had already gone out.
screens.why2: Text only is plain, but 'Every answer in a quiet room. More than 9 in 10 where it is loud' never says what is being counted, so I have to read it twice and still guess it means the voice is understood correctly.
screens.why3: I know my reservation agents and directors are on shift, on phones or at noisy desks, so I can decide from what I know how they would best answer.
screens.why4: AI interviewer, text and let them choose are complete and distinct, but the AI option is cluttered with the unclear accuracy fragment and the trailing 'Hear it' and credits labels.
screens.why5: My 'Text only' pick is kept as I chose it, and nothing on this delivery screen changes what I typed about Codyco.
screens.instead: How should they answer? AI interviewer: a face on video asks each question aloud, and they talk, type or tap; it understands speech reliably in a quiet room, slightly less in a noisy one (needs Keel's credits). Text only: they read each question and tap or type. Let them choose: they pick when they open the link (needs Keel's credits).

screens.why1: Right after choosing how people answer, the last thing to settle before sending is who receives the link, so it is obvious why it comes here.
screens.why2: The three options read plainly on first pass to a founder who sells to hotel groups, and only 'Contacts page' assumes a little knowledge of Keel, which the sentence itself explains.
screens.why3: I know whether I have named reservation agents and revenue directors to send to, so I can answer this from my own pipeline.
screens.why4: The three routes are distinct and cover my case, but 'People I found with Keel' also ends with me sending each person a link, so it overlaps a little with the first option, and nothing says what to do if I have no one yet.
screens.why5: Nothing I typed is changed, and my pick of people I know by name is offered in nearly those words.

screens.why1: As the first question on a link sent cold, it is obvious that they are checking whether I am the right kind of person before going further.
screens.why2: Hotel group, central reservations office and call center are everyday words in my job, so I can answer on first reading.
screens.why3: I know without guessing whether my own group runs a central reservations office or call center in Germany.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover this cleanly, and a gate question needs no escape chip.
screens.why5: It keeps the founder's segment of German hotel groups with a central reservations office or call center and tells me nothing about any product.
screens.why6: It is one short question of under 20 words, with no symbols or abbreviations, and I can answer yes or no after hearing it once.

screens.why1: After confirming I run a central reservations setup, showing me the idea before asking buying questions makes obvious sense, and the kicker says that is what comes next.
screens.why2: I follow it on first reading since OPERA Cloud and booking system are my daily words, but "answers in the hotel's voice" is vague (a cloned voice, or just our greeting and tone?), and "by rules you set" needs a second thought.
screens.why3: Missed calls, after-hours cover, payment at booking and OPERA are all things I know and manage, so I can weigh this from my own operation.
screens.why4: The screen is a card to read and shows no options, so this does not apply.
screens.why5: The card is shown on purpose and nothing leaks, but "your reservation agents forward the calls" reads oddly because forwarding is set up in the phone system rather than done by agents, and it assumes every hotel uses OPERA Cloud.
screens.why6: The short sentences say well, but it is a lot to hold at one hearing, the colon before "OPERA Cloud" does not say well, and the last sentence repeats a long clause almost word for word.
screens.instead: Imagine Codyco. Calls nobody picks up are forwarded to Codyco, which answers in your hotel's name, answers the guest's questions and takes the payment. It writes the confirmed booking straight into OPERA Cloud and passes calls to your desk by rules you set. The people building it believe it would turn missed calls into confirmed bookings.

screens.why1: Right after the idea card about answering booking calls, it makes sense to ask how many calls we lose today, because that is what any tool like this would have to pay for itself against.
screens.why2: I understand it on first reading, but "lose" is loose: it could mean calls nobody answered, callers who hung up in the queue, or calls that ended without a booking, and those give me different figures.
screens.why3: I track this rate as revenue director and can give my figure for last month, about 6%, without guessing.
screens.why4: The number box and "Nothing" work and "I don't know" fits, but the label says "per hotel a month" while the question asks about my team, and across a central office I have one group-wide rate, not a per-hotel one.
screens.why5: It stays with calls that go unanswered or are lost, in words a reservations office would use, and nothing of the founder's product or plan reaches me.
screens.why6: It is short, one question and easy to answer by ear, but the spoken escape is "I don't know" rather than the fixed "I can't recall", and the screen's "Nothing" chip and per-hotel unit are not said.
screens.instead: Last month, about what share of your reservation calls went unanswered or were abandoned before anyone picked up? Box: % of reservation calls last month; escape: I can't recall.

screens.why1: After the idea card and the question about lost calls, it makes sense to ask me what this is worth, and pricing tools is my decision.
screens.why2: Setup fee, monthly fee and per-hotel pricing are how I already compare booking tools, so I understand this on first reading, even if 'worth' is softer than 'pay'.
screens.why3: I choose and pay for tools like this and budget them per property, so I can answer from experience, though the exact figure for a new product is partly an estimate.
screens.why4: The ranges share endpoints (€3,000 and €5,000 each sit in two bands), and 'I wouldn't pay for this' misstates my answer if I would pay monthly but nothing up front, since no option says that.
screens.why5: The card on purpose gives me the name Codyco and the question uses only that name and plain pricing terms, with no founder jargon or talk of roles reaching me.
screens.why6: It can be said and an ordered ladder is easy to follow, but six long options repeating 'per hotel' run past the five-point limit, are read at once instead of in two steps, and the monthly part drops the spoken escape.
screens.instead: What would you pay up front per hotel, if anything? Nothing up front; under €1,000; €1,000 to under €3,000; €3,000 to under €5,000; €5,000 to under €10,000; or €10,000 or more, asked in two spoken steps with the 'I wouldn't pay for this' answer kept for the monthly question, and 'I can't say' as the escape on both.

screens.why1: Right after asking what this is worth to me per hotel, it makes sense to ask how my group actually funded the last tool, because that shows whether the money would really be there.
screens.why2: I talk about budget lines and sign-offs every year in hotel group budgeting, so I understand this on first reading.
screens.why3: I decide on and pay for these tools, so I know exactly where the money for the last one came from.
screens.why4: The first three options are distinct and in my words, but 'There was no budget for it' overlaps with 'Taken from other spending', since a tool with no budget still got paid for from somewhere.
screens.why5: It asks only about my own last purchase, and nothing of the founder's product or terms appears on this screen.
screens.why6: Two short sentences, with four short options I can hold after one hearing and a single escape said last, though the anchor and the question together are slightly more than one breath.
screens.instead: Think of the last tool your team paid for. Where did the money come from? A budget line we already had; a new budget line someone signed off; or taken from other spending. Or say I can't recall one.

screens.why1: Right after asking where the money came from and what it would be worth per hotel, it makes sense to ask whether I could approve this amount myself.
screens.why2: "Sign off" and the amount are clear on first reading, but "the hotel's owner" is not how I think about approval at a hotel group, where it goes to the group's managing director or CFO.
screens.why3: I know my own approval limit and who has to agree above it, though I would need to work out the total across our hotels because the figure is per hotel.
screens.why4: The owner, several people and someone else's decision overlap, group management is not named, and "I can't recall one" does not fit a question about what I could approve.
screens.why5: It stays a plain question about who approves the money, with nothing of the product or the founder's terms for people reaching me.
screens.why6: The stem is short and says well, but three options starting with "No" blur together when heard, and "I can't recall one" sounds odd because there is nothing to recall.
screens.instead: Could you approve about €3,000 per hotel across the group yourself, or would someone else have to agree? Options: Yes, I could approve it myself; No, group management would have to agree; No, the hotel's owner would have to agree; No, several people would have to agree. Escape: I can't tell.

screens.why1: After asking about price and who signs off, it is obvious to ask what else could hold up the purchase, and for a tool touching guest calls in Germany that is data protection.
screens.why2: A data protection review is everyday language for a German hotel group revenue director, and I understand the question on first reading.
screens.why3: I know guest calls would raise data protection questions, but whether a review is needed and how long it takes is partly a guess because our data protection officer handles it and I have not bought this exact product.
screens.why4: The three options are distinct and in my words, but 'I can't recall' is an odd escape for a hypothetical purchase, where the honest answer is 'I can't tell' or 'I don't know'.
screens.why5: Codyco was already introduced on the idea card, and nothing new about the product or the founder's terms reaches me here.
screens.why6: It is one short question with three short options I can hold after one hearing, and the escape is said last.
screens.instead: If you bought Codyco, would it need a data protection review of guest calls first? Yes, and it would take a long time; Yes, but it would be quick; or No, it wouldn't be needed. Or say I can't tell.

screens.why1: After the sign-off and data protection questions, asking what else would slow a purchase is the obvious next step, though "One more thing" gives it no link to what I just answered.
screens.why2: Short and in plain words; I know at once it means what holds up a purchase at our group, and Codyco is the name from the card I was shown.
screens.why3: I run tool purchases for a hotel group, so I know where the weeks go: the works council, IT, the data protection officer and contract terms.
screens.why4: A box to type in, with no options, rows or chips to judge.
screens.why5: It stays on the buying friction and uses only the product name already shown on the idea card, with nothing new about the founder's plans or roles reaching me.
screens.why6: Nine plain words, one question, nothing that only the eye can read, so I can hear it once and start talking.

screens.why1: After the worth, budget, sign-off and data protection questions, asking whether I would actually pay for a pilot is the obvious last step.
screens.why2: A paid pilot at one hotel with the money back is plain to me as a revenue director, though the card never says what would earn the money back.
screens.why3: I choose and pay for these tools, so I can answer from how I would treat this spend at one of our hotels.
screens.why4: Yes, Probably not and No cover the answers I would give, but Probably not is a hedge with no matching Probably yes, so a cautious yes has nowhere to go and the top option is far longer than the others.
screens.why5: The product name comes from the idea card shown on purpose, and the price and money-back pilot read as a clear offer with nothing internal leaking to me.
screens.why6: It is one short question that says well, but the yes option repeats the whole stem including €3,000 in a mouthful, while the other two are two words and one word.
screens.instead: If it were ready today, would you pay €3,000 for a money-back pilot at one hotel, or not? Yes, I'd pay; Probably not; or No.
